title: 1 Samuel 12:1–15
context: 1 Samuel 12:1–15 is Samuel’s farewell address at Gilgal. He asks the people to testify that he has not defrauded or oppressed anyone, and they agree. He then reviews the LORD’s righteous acts from the exodus through the judges and charges that Israel asked for a king when the LORD was their king. Yet the LORD has set a king over them, and the future of both people and king depends on whether they fear the LORD, serve him, and listen to his voice. Arminian and Reformed readers agree on the covenant structure of blessing and warning, and they read the conditional promises of 12:14–15 with different emphases about perseverance and the grace that enables it.

verses.text: Samuel said to all Israel, “Behold, I have listened to your voice in all that you said to me, and have made a king over you.
verses.arminianNotes: Samuel tells Israel that he has listened to their voice and made a king over them. Arminian readers see Samuel accepting the people’s choice, even though he had warned against it (8:10–18), and see God allowing his people’s decision while holding them responsible for it.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed interpreters agree and note that the LORD had told Samuel to listen to the people (8:7, 22). Both traditions read the verse as introducing a covenant address in which God’s rule and the people’s request are set side by side.

verses.text: Now, behold, the king walks before you. I am old and gray-headed. Behold, my sons are with you. I have walked before you from my youth to this day.
verses.arminianNotes: Samuel says the king now walks before them, while he is old and gray, his sons are among them, and he has walked before them from his youth. Arminians see a faithful servant stepping aside and pointing to a lifetime of integrity as he hands leadership on.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree. The mention of his sons may recall their failures (8:3–5) that prompted the request for a king. Both traditions read Samuel’s words as a transition from the judges’ era to the monarchy.

verses.text: Here I am. Witness against me before the LORD and before his anointed. Whose ox have I taken? Whose donkey have I taken? Whom have I defrauded? Whom have I oppressed? Of whose hand have I taken a bribe to make me blind my eyes? I will restore it to you.”
verses.arminianNotes: Samuel invites the people to testify before the LORD and his anointed whether he has taken anyone’s ox or donkey, defrauded, oppressed, or taken a bribe. Arminian readers see the standard of integrity expected of leaders, and they see Samuel’s openness as an example of accountability.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed interpreters agree and note the echo of Moses’ defense in Numbers 16:15. Both traditions contrast Samuel’s conduct with the taking that the king would do (8:11–17) and read the verse as a model for leadership among God’s people.

verses.text: They said, “You have not defrauded us, nor oppressed us, neither have you taken anything from anyone’s hand.”
verses.arminianNotes: The people answer that he has not defrauded, oppressed, or taken anything from anyone. Arminians see the people’s public confirmation as vindicating Samuel, and they see his record as a witness that God’s appointed leaders can serve faithfully.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and observe that the people’s answer repeats Samuel’s questions, confirming his integrity point by point. Both traditions see the verse as establishing that the people’s request for a king was not caused by Samuel’s failure.

verses.text: He said to them, “The LORD is witness against you, and his anointed is witness today, that you have not found anything in my hand.” They said, “He is witness.”
verses.arminianNotes: Samuel says the LORD and his anointed are witnesses that they have found nothing in his hand, and they answer, "He is witness." Arminians see a solemn legal setting in which the people affirm Samuel’s innocence before God.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed interpreters agree and see the witness formula as part of a covenant lawsuit form in the chapter. Both traditions read the verse as preparing for Samuel’s charge against the people, since his record is now established.

verses.text: Samuel said to the people, “It is the LORD who appointed Moses and Aaron, and that brought your fathers up out of the land of Egypt.
verses.arminianNotes: Samuel says it is the LORD who appointed Moses and Aaron and brought the fathers out of Egypt. Arminian readers see Samuel directing the people’s attention away from himself and the king to the LORD, who has always provided their leaders.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and stress that the history to follow is God’s history. Both traditions read the verse as the start of a review of the LORD’s saving acts, which grounds Israel’s covenant obligations in his grace.

verses.text: Now therefore stand still, that I may plead with you before the LORD concerning all the righteous acts of the LORD, which he did to you and to your fathers.
verses.arminianNotes: Samuel calls the people to stand still while he pleads with them before the LORD about his righteous acts. Arminians see the call to remember God’s faithful deeds as a call to respond to him rightly now.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed interpreters agree and note the legal language of pleading. Both traditions read "the righteous acts of the LORD" as his saving acts on behalf of his people, the same theme found in the Song of Deborah (Judges 5:11).

verses.text: “When Jacob had come into Egypt, and your fathers cried to the LORD, then the LORD sent Moses and Aaron, who brought your fathers out of Egypt, and made them to dwell in this place.
verses.arminianNotes: When Jacob went into Egypt and the fathers cried out, the LORD sent Moses and Aaron, who brought them out and settled them in this place. Arminians see God hearing his people’s cry and acting to save them, the pattern of his mercy.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and see the summary as compressing the story from Genesis to Joshua into one sentence. Both traditions see God’s initiative in sending deliverers as the heart of Israel’s history.

verses.text: But they forgot the LORD their God; and he sold them into the hand of Sisera, captain of the army of Hazor, and into the hand of the Philistines, and into the hand of the king of Moab; and they fought against them.
verses.arminianNotes: They forgot the LORD, and he sold them into the hands of Sisera, the Philistines, and the king of Moab. Arminian readers see the consequences of forgetting God as just discipline that follows his people’s choices.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed interpreters agree and stress that the LORD "sold" them, so their defeats were under his rule. Both traditions read the verse as summarizing the cycle of Judges (Judges 3–5) and see the oppression as discipline intended to bring Israel back.

verses.text: They cried to the LORD, and said, ‘We have sinned, because we have forsaken the LORD and have served the Baals and the Ashtaroth; but now deliver us out of the hand of our enemies, and we will serve you.’
verses.arminianNotes: They cried out, confessing that they had sinned by serving the Baals and the Ashtaroth, and asked to be delivered so they would serve him. Arminians see genuine confession and turning back to God as the response God welcomes.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and note that the confession recalls Judges 10:10. Both traditions read the verse as showing God’s willingness to hear confession, and both note that the pattern of Judges is one of repeated relapse after deliverance.

verses.text: The LORD sent Jerubbaal, Bedan, Jephthah, and Samuel, and delivered you out of the hand of your enemies on every side; and you lived in safety.
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD sent Jerubbaal, Bedan, Jephthah, and Samuel, and delivered them so they lived in safety. Arminians see God’s faithfulness in repeatedly raising deliverers. Bedan is otherwise unknown, and some ancient versions read Barak, while some also read Samson in place of Samuel.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed interpreters agree on the point of the verse and treat the name questions as unresolved textual issues. Both traditions read the list as evidence that the LORD had always provided for his people’s safety, without needing a human king.

verses.text: “When you saw that Nahash the king of the children of Ammon came against you, you said to me, ‘No, but a king shall reign over us,’ when the LORD your God was your king.
verses.arminianNotes: When Nahash came, the people said, "No, but a king shall reign over us," when the LORD their God was their king. Arminians see the people’s request as a failure to trust the LORD’s rule, choosing a visible human solution instead.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and connect the verse with 8:7, where the LORD says they have rejected him as king. Both traditions note that the verse links the request with the Ammonite threat, and both read it as exposing a lack of faith in God’s kingship.

verses.text: Now therefore see the king whom you have chosen and whom you have asked for. Behold, the LORD has set a king over you.
verses.arminianNotes: Samuel presents the king they chose and asked for, and says the LORD has set a king over them. Arminians see the verse holding together the people’s real choice and God’s response, since God grants the request and works within it.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed interpreters agree and stress that even a king chosen in sinful motives is set in place by the LORD. Both traditions read the verse as showing God’s sovereignty over human decisions without excusing the people’s request.

verses.text: If you will fear the LORD, and serve him, and listen to his voice, and not rebel against the commandment of the LORD, then both you and also the king who reigns over you are followers of the LORD your God.
verses.arminianNotes: If the people fear the LORD, serve him, listen to his voice, and do not rebel, then both people and king will follow the LORD. Arminian readers see a real condition placed on the covenant people: their continued blessing depends on continued faithful response, and the warning in 12:15 is a genuine possibility.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree that the condition is real and that obedience is required. They also read such conditions as the means by which God calls his people to the faithfulness he works in them (compare Deuteronomy 30:6), so the condition and God’s commitment in 12:22 are held together. Both traditions note that the verse addresses Israel and its king as a nation under covenant, not individual salvation directly.

verses.text: But if you will not listen to the LORD’s voice, but rebel against the commandment of the LORD, then the LORD’s hand will be against you, as it was against your fathers.
verses.arminianNotes: If they do not listen and rebel, the LORD’s hand will be against them, as against their fathers. Arminians see the warning as the counterpart of 12:14, showing that God’s people can bring discipline on themselves by turning from him.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed interpreters agree and read the warning as a real threat of covenant discipline. Both traditions read the verse in light of the judges’ history just reviewed, where God’s hand was against Israel when they forsook him (12:9).
